###### Abstract

While Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is the prevailing method for
equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with function calling
capabilities, its effectiveness is often compromised by two critical
challenges: 1) Imbalanced Training Signals, where lengthy
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning tokens dominate the training signals
over concise function calls in the learning objective, and 2) Imbalanced
Data Hardness, characterized by a scarcity of hard training examples. To
overcome these limitations, we propose Balanced Supervised Fine-tuning
(BalanceSFT), a novel framework incorporates two key components: a
Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss that employs a learnable
hyperparameter to dynamically adjust the token contributions of CoT
reasoning and function calls, together with a Hard Data Re-sampling
(HDR) strategy that establishes a feedback loop to selectively generate
new, high-quality complex data guided by model errors. Extensive
experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed BalanceSFT
framework. With BalanceSFT, a 7B model achieves function calling
performance on par with state-of-the-art giants like GPT-4o. Our code,
models, and dataset are open-sourced.

## 1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has marked a
transformative era in natural language processing [Ouyang et al.
(2022)](#bib.bib35); [Achiam et al. (2023)](#bib.bib52); [Touvron et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib53); [Bai et al. (2023)](#bib.bib36), demonstrating
exceptional capabilities in text understanding, generation, and complex
reasoning [Zhong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib38). A pivotal direction in
enhancing their practicality is equipping them with function calling
abilities, enabling LLMs to interact with external tools and APIs to
execute concrete actions and access real-world data [WANG et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib42); [Singh et al. (2024)](#bib.bib41). Supervised
Fine-Tuning (SFT) has emerged as the standard paradigm to instill this
capability, typically by training models on demonstrations that combine
a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning process with the final function
call [Lightman et al. (2023)](#bib.bib34); [Guo et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib51); [Team et al. (2025)](#bib.bib39).

![Refer to caption](2505.20192v3/intro1.png)

Figure 1: Two challenges in LLM Function Calling. (a) Imbalanced
Training Signals: The lengthy Chain-of-Thought (CoT) tokens dominate the
learning signal, overshadowing the concise but critical function call.
(b) Imbalanced Data Hardness: The training dataset is dominated by
simple examples, with a scarcity of hard cases necessary for robust
performance.

Despite the remarkable progress, conventional SFT approaches suffer from
two inherent and critical imbalances that severely limit its
effectiveness [Ju et al. (2024)](#bib.bib21). On the one hand, as
illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
the training signals are skewed due to a token-level imbalance. In a
typical function-calling sample, the lengthy CoT reasoning tokens
numerically dominate the concise, yet critical, function call
tokens [Qian et al. (2025)](#bib.bib50). This Imbalanced Training Signal
causes the model to be optimized primarily for generating plausible
reasoning, often at the expense of precision in the final tool
execution. On the other hand, the data distribution is characterized by
an Imbalanced Data Hardness [Li et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23); [Zhang et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib54). Existing training datasets are naturally
dominated by simple examples, while complex and challenging cases that
are crucial for robust performance are scarce. This scarcity prevents
the model from effectively learning to handle edge cases and intricate
scenarios [Zeng et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib30).

To tackle the dual challenges, we propose Balanced Supervised
Fine-Tuning (BalanceSFT), a novel framework designed to recalibrate the
SFT process. BalanceSFT incorporates two simple yet effective
components: 1) A Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss function that
introduces a learnable hyperparameter to dynamically balance the
contribution of CoT tokens and function call tokens to the total loss,
ensuring that the model does not overlook the critical execution step; 2) A Hard Data Re-sampling (HDR) strategy that establishes a feedback
loop to generate new, high-quality complex data guided by model errors.
Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our BalanceSFT
framework. The results show that a 7B model trained with BalanceSFT
achieves tool-calling performance competitive with state-of-the-art
giants like GPT-4o [Hurst et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28) on the
comprehensive Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [Patil et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib48) and other specialized benchmarks [Chen et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib24); [Li et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23).

Our main contributions are threefold:

- •
  We identify two critical yet overlooked limitations in standard SFT
  for tool learning: the imbalance in training signals between lengthy
  reasoning and concise function calls, and the imbalance in data
  hardness.
- •
  We propose BalanceSFT, a novel framework that introduces a
  Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss and a Hard Data Re-sampling
  (HDR) strategy to calibrate the learning focus.
- •
  We train a 7B model with the proposed BalanceSFT framework, achieving
  tool-calling performance comparable to the state-of-the-art model like
  GPT-4o.

## 2 Related Work

Function Calling for LLMs. The ability of LLMs to interact with external
tools and APIs through function calling has emerged as a crucial aspect
of their practical utility [Wang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib40); [Singh et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib41); [Patil et al. (2024)](#bib.bib48). This
capability allows LLMs to transcend the limitations of solely processing
and generating text, enabling them to ground their responses in
real-world data and automate complex tasks [Wang et al.
(2024a)](#bib.bib32); [Kavathekar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib33); [Zhang et
al. (2025a)](#bib.bib55). Early explorations in this area focused on
enabling LLMs to understand descriptions of functions and generate the
necessary calls with appropriate parameters [Wang et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib20); [Zheng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib19). By training LLMs
on datasets specifically curated for function calling scenarios, these
methods aim to instill a deeper understanding of function semantics and
parameter requirements [Prabhakar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib43); [Zeng et
al. (2025b)](#bib.bib30). The quality and diversity of these fine-tuning
datasets play a critical role in the resulting performance of the LLMs
in function calling tasks. RL has also been explored as a means to
optimize LLMs for function calling [Zhang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib49);
[Qian et al. (2025)](#bib.bib50). RL-based approaches often involve
defining reward functions that incentivize the generation of correct and
executable function calls. While RL offers the potential to directly
optimize for task success, it still severe sparse reward and the lack of
effective data [Qu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib16); [Zeng et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib18).

Improving Reasoning Capability via SFT. The integration of CoT with
function calling mechanisms holds substantial promise for enhancing the
accuracy and reliability of tool-use [Lu et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14);
[Kokane et al. ()](#bib.bib13); [Chen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib12). By
reasoning through the user’s request and identifying the most
appropriate course of action, including the selection of relevant tools
and their parameters, the model can make more informed decisions about
function invocation [Li (2025)](#bib.bib11); [Shen (2024)](#bib.bib10).
The explicit reasoning process provided by CoT can also improve the
transparency and interpretability of the model’s actions [Wu et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib9); [Dong et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8). However, the
integration of CoT into the training process for function calling
introduces a unique challenge related to the design of the loss
function [Yang et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib4). Traditional training
methodologies, primarily SFT, typically treat the entire generated
sequence (including the reasoning process and the final function call)
uniformly when calculating the loss [Lobo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib5).
This can lead to an imbalance, where the potentially lengthy sequences
of reasoning steps dominate the loss calculation, potentially
overshadowing the importance of the final, often shorter, function call.
Consequently, the model might be incentivized to generate elaborate and
seemingly plausible reasoning chains [Agarwal et al. (2024)](#bib.bib7);
[Chen et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib6), even if they do not ultimately lead to
a correct or executable function call. This inherent tension between the
verbose reasoning process and the need for a succinct and precise
function call necessitates a more nuanced approach to loss function
design that can effectively balance these two critical aspects of the
task. Our work addresses this challenge by introducing a Self-adjusted
Signal Balancing approach that explicitly considers the different roles
and importance of the reasoning process and the final function execution
during training.

## 3 Method

In this section, we elaborate on our proposed Balanced Supervised
Fine-Tuning (BalanceSFT) framework, which is designed to address the
dual challenges of Imbalanced Training Signals and Imbalanced Data
Hardness.

![Refer to caption](2505.20192v3/main1.png)

Figure 2: Overview of the BalanceSFT framework. It starts with a
standard function call dataset, which is refined through a Base Quality
Check and Answer Check to create initial training data and identify hard
data. The model is first initialized via a Cold Start using the
Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) Loss. Subsequently, the Hard Data
Re-sampling (HDR) strategy creates a Self-evolving Loop where the model
iteratively reasons on hard cases, generates new solutions, and
undergoes quality-gated retraining.

### 3.1 Overview

The overall architecture of our BalanceSFT framework is illustrated in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Method ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness").
It consists of two core components that work in synergy: 1) A
Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss that dynamically balances the
learning signals between lengthy Chain-of-Thought reasoning tokens and
concise function call tokens during training, and a Hard Data
Re-sampling (HDR) strategy that establishes a feedback loop to
selectively generate and utilize high-quality complex data based on
model errors. These two components address the signal imbalance and data
hardness imbalance, respectively, forming a comprehensive solution for
robust function calling capability.

### 3.2 Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) Loss

Motivation and Analysis. We conduct an intuitive analysis of a CoT
Dataset. As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) Loss ‣ 3 Method ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
a CoT Dataset distilled from QwQ-32B [Team (2024)](#bib.bib37) based on
the open-sourced function call dataset xlam-function-calling-60k [Zhang
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54), which exhibits a significant token
imbalance: Chain-of-Thought reasoning segments contain approximately 10
times more tokens (mean=350.74) than function call results (mean=31.07).
This substantial disparity highlights the need to rebalance the training
focus toward the short but critical function execution components.

|             |                |        |                   |        |
| ----------- | -------------- | ------ | ----------------- | ------ |
| Dataset     | CoT Token Len. |        | Result Token Len. |        |
|             | Mean           | Median | Mean              | Median |
| CoT Dataset | 350.74         | 248.00 | 31.07             | 27.00  |

Table 1: Token Statistics of the CoT Dataset for function call. Note the
approximately 10x higher token count for the CoT compared to the final
execution.

Formulation. The output of an LLM $`\mathcal{M}`$ can be decomposed into
two components: chain-of-thought $`t`$ and the final function calling
execution $`f`$. Let $`N_{t}`$ and $`N_{f}`$ denote the token counts for
these components, respectively, with $`N_{\text{all}}=N_{t}+N_{f}`$
representing the total tokens, and $`V`$ represents the size of the
vocabulary. The standard SFT loss can be expressed as a weighted sum:

|     |                                  |                                                                                        |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle L_{\text{SFT}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N_{all}}\sum_{j=1}^{V}-p_{ij}\log p_{ij}}{N_{all}}`$ |     | (1) |

We decompose the loss $`L_{\text{STF}}`$ as following:

|     |                                  |                                                                                                                                  |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle L_{\text{STF}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{N_{t}}{N_{\text{all}}}\cdot\frac{1}{N_{t}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\sum_{j=1}^{V}-p_{ij}\log p_{ij}`$             |     | (2) |
|     |                                  | $`\displaystyle+\frac{N_{f}}{N_{\text{all}}}\cdot\frac{1}{N_{f}}\sum_{i=N_{t}+1}^{N_{t}+N_{f}}\sum_{j=1}^{V}-p_{ij}\log p_{ij}`$ |     |     |
|     |                                  | $`\displaystyle=w_{t}\cdot L_{\text{think}}+w_{f}\cdot L_{\text{result}}`$                                                       |     |     |

where
$`w_{t}=\frac{N_{t}}{N_{\text{all}}},w_{f}=\frac{N_{f}}{N_{\text{all}}}`$,
thus $`w_{t}+w_{f}=1`$. Let $`L_{\text{think}}`$ and
$`L_{\text{result}}`$ represent the loss for reasoning and function call
components, respectively.

The statistical analysis from
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) Loss ‣ 3 Method ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness")
reveals that $`N_{t}\gg N_{f}`$, which implies $`w_{t}\gg w_{f}`$ during
standard training. This naturally leads to the model being optimized
primarily for generating plausible reasoning at the expense of precise
function execution. To address this inherent imbalance, we propose the
Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
L_{\text{SSB}}=\alpha\cdot L_{\text{think}}+(1-\alpha)\cdot L_{\text{result}}
``` |  | (3) |

where $`\alpha`$ is a learnable parameter with $`\alpha\in[0,1]`$. The
introduction of $`\alpha`$ allows the model to dynamically adjust its
focus between reasoning depth and execution accuracy based on
performance requirements. In practice, we set $`\alpha`$ as a trainable
parameter to avoid extensive hyperparameter tuning.

### 3.3 Hard Data Re-sampling (HDR) Strategy

The core objective of the HDR strategy is to address the Imbalanced Data
Hardness issue through a carefully designed self-evolving data
refinement loop. This process can be formally described as a sequence of
iterative data filtration and augmentation operations. Let
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{initial}}`$ denote the initial training dataset.
Each data point $`d_{i}=(q_{i},c_{i},f_{i})`$ consists of a user query
$`q_{i}`$, a CoT reasoning sequence $`c_{i}`$, and a function call
$`f_{i}`$.

Data Filtration via Quality Checks. The dataset undergoes a two-stage
filtration process defined by boolean functions $`\text{BQC}(\cdot)`$
and $`\text{AC}(\cdot)`$ for Base Quality Check (including response,
query, and CoT identification) and Answer Check (including function,
parameter, and format verification), respectively:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\text{qualified}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\,d_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{initial}}\mid\text{BQC}(d_{i})\!\land\!\text{AC}(d_{i})\,\},`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\,d_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{initial}}\mid\text{BQC}(d_{i})\!\land\!\neg\text{AC}(d_{i})\,\}.`$ |  |  |

Here, $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{qualified}}`$ is used for the Cold Start
phase to initialize the model $`\mathcal{M}_{0}`$, while
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}`$ is reserved for iterative self-evolution.

Self-Evolving Loop. The model at iteration $`t`$, denoted as
$`\mathcal{M}_{t}`$, is used to reason on the current hard dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t}`$, generating a new set of candidate
responses $`\mathcal{R}^{t+1}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}^{t+1}=\{\mathcal{M}_{t}(q_{i})\mid\forall q_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t}\}
``` |  | (5) |

Each candidate response $`r_{j}\in\mathcal{R}^{t+1}`$ is evaluated by an
ensemble of LLM judges $`\mathcal{J}=\{J_{1},J_{2},\dots,J_{k}\}`$
(e.g., Gemini-2.5-Pro [Comanici et al. (2025)](#bib.bib29),
GPT-4o [Hurst et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28), Claude-3.5 sonnet [Claude
()](#bib.bib27)) via majority voting. The scoring function
$`\text{Score}(r_{j})`$ aggregates their judgments:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Score}(r_{j})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{m=1}^{k}\mathbb{I}\left(J_{m}(r_{j})\geq\tau\right)
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\mathbb{I}(\cdot)`$ is the indicator function and $`\tau`$ is a
passing threshold. Responses meeting the quality standard form the new
high-quality dataset:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}^{t}=\{r_{j}\in\mathcal{R}^{t+1}\mid\text{Score}(r_{j})=1\}
``` |  | (7) |

The model is then fine-tuned on this newly generated data:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{M}_{t+1}=\text{SFT}\left(\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{D}_{\text{new}}^{t}\right)
``` |  | (8) |

Simultaneously, the hard dataset is updated by retaining failed samples:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t+1}=\{d_{i}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t}\mid\text{Score}(\mathcal{M}_{t}(q_{i}))<1\}
``` |  | (9) |

This iterative process continues until convergence criteria are met:
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t+1}=\emptyset`$ or $`t=T_{\text{max}}`$.

The entire HDR strategy establishes a virtuous cycle where model
improvement and data quality enhancement reinforce each other,
effectively resolving the data hardness imbalance through the iterative
refinement process:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{M}_{t+1},\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t+1}=\text{HDR-Iteration}(\mathcal{M}_{t},\mathcal{D}_{\text{hard}}^{t})
``` |  | (10) |

## 4 Experiments

The experiments of this paper are divided into five parts. The first
part introduces the Experiment setting. The second part elaborates on
the Data Preparation. In the third part, we compare the BalanceSFT
models with current powerful models and function call specialized models
on the BFCL benchmark  [Patil et al. (2024)](#bib.bib48) and other
specialized benchmarks. In the fourth part, we present an ablation
study, while the final part provides further insights into the proposed
method.

### 4.1 Experiment Setting

Dataset. As shown in
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.2 Data Preparation ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
our training dataset comprises two components:
xlam-function-calling-60k [Zhang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib54) and
Open-Agentic-tool-use [Aworld team, inclusionAI (2025)](#bib.bib22).
xlam-function-calling-60k contains 60000 samples from 3,673 APIs across
21 categories, while Open-Agentic-tool-use includes 30000 samples from
129 APIs across 8 categories. The former focuses on single-turn tool-use
to strengthen the model’s basic capabilities, while the latter focuses
on multi-turn tool-use to address complex scenario requirements. The
training dataset we adopted covers thousands of APIs from multiple
categories, helping the model learn cross-domain API matching logic and
improve its generalization ability. The distribution of the diverse and
comprehensive API resources is shown in
Figure [5](#A1.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
and the details of the dataset are further illustrated and analyzed in
Appendix [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness").

Benchmarks. To assess our methodology, we choose a highly representative
benchmark, the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL)  [Patil et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib48). For BFCL, we conduct evaluations on BFCLv3,
which contains single-turn and multi-turn function calling scenarios.
Performance across all subsets of BFCL is reported in terms of accuracy
(%). We further evaluate our model on two specialized tool-use
benchmarks, ACEBench [Chen et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib24) and APIBank [Li
et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23).

Backbones. To demonstrate the effectiveness and general applicability of
our BalanceSFT framework, we select Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Inst [Hui et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib45) as our primary base model. To demonstrate the
effectiveness of our method, we also conduct additional experiments
using Llama-3.2-3B-Inst [Touvron et al. (2023)](#bib.bib53).

Baselines. For comprehensive comparison, we include both open-source and
closed-source models: open-source models include
Moonshotai-Kimi-K2-Instruct [Team et al. (2025)](#bib.bib39),
DeepSeek-R1-0528 [Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib51),
Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 [Yang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib17),
ToolACE-MT (8B) [Zeng et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib30), and BitAgent-8B 
[(2024)](#bib.bib25); closed-source models include GPT-5 [OpenAI
(2025)](#bib.bib3), GPT-4o [Hurst et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28),
Gemini-2.5-Pro [Comanici et al. (2025)](#bib.bib29), and Grok-4 [xAI
(2025)](#bib.bib26).

Implementation Details. Our implementations are based on the training
framework LLaMA Factory [Zheng et al. (2024)](#bib.bib44). To ensure
fair comparison, we maintain consistent hyperparameters across all
experiments: batch size of 512, learning rate of $`4\times 10^{-5}`$,
warm-up rate of 0.05. The SSB loss hyperparameter $`\alpha`$ is
initialized to 0.7 and set as a learnable parameter. During inference,
we set the number of inferences to 3 with a temperature 0.7. In HDR, for
the LLM-as-judge phase, we use Gemini-2.5-Pro [Comanici et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib29), GPT-4o [Hurst et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28),
Claude-3.5 Sonnet [Claude ()](#bib.bib27) as judges with the same
temperature setting at 0.7, threshold $`\tau=0.5`$, and scoring range
\[0, 1\]. The maximum iteration $`T_{max}`$ is 10. All trainings run on
8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs.

### 4.2 Data Preparation

We construct two CoT datasets: (1) Strategy CoT, generated by GPT-4o
following prescribed reasoning strategies, and (2) Natural CoT,
generated by QwQ-32B [Team (2024)](#bib.bib37) based on its natural
reasoning process (implemented with vLLM [Kwon et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib2), temperature = 0.1). We conduct standard SFT on
Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Inst using each dataset. As shown in
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setting ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
we observe that Natural CoT consistently outperforms Strategy CoT.
Therefore, we adopt Natural CoT for cold-start data generation and
employ self-inference in the Hard Data Re-sampling (HDR) stage to
maintain model-consistent reasoning patterns.

### 4.3 Main Results

The performance of BalanceSFT-7B (built upon Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Inst) on
the BFCL benchmark is summarized in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setting ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness").
We report accuracy across the main subsets using the official BFCL
evaluation script.

Multi-Turn Evaluation. The Multi-Turn subset evaluates a model’s ability
to handle complex, continuous conversations. As shown in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setting ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
BalanceSFT-7B demonstrates the strongest overall capability, leading the
Overall score with 47.00. It also ensures optimal performance in the key
failure mode categories: Miss Function at 47.00 and Miss Parameter at
41.00, indicating the ability to keenly detect the absence of functions
and required parameters in the dialogue flow. In contrast, the Long
Context metric, which tests memory and coherence over conversation
history, is led by the closed-source model GPT-4o-2024-11-20 [Hurst et
al. (2024)](#bib.bib28) at 51.00, with BalanceSFT-7B being the second
best at 46.50.

Single-Turn Evaluation. The Single-Turn subset focuses on isolated
prompts under Non-Live and Live settings. As reported in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.1 Experiment Setting ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
BalanceSFT-7B maintains its competitive edge by achieving the highest
Overall score of 84.00. The Non-Live metric is led by
Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 [Yang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib17) with the
highest score of 90.12. For the Live metric, simulating the real-world
interactions, DeepSeek-R1-0528[Guo et al. (2025)](#bib.bib51) performs
the best at 80.90, with BalanceSFT-7B coming in a close second at 79.70.

Despite being a small model, BalanceSFT-7B outperforms larger
proprietary and specialized models, revealing that our BalanceSFT
strategy achieves superior performance, particularly in the multi-turn
function calling scenario. These findings demonstrate that BalanceSFT-7B
can accurately analyze system status and remains highly sensitive to key
functions and parameters within context.

generalization, ranking first and second on the Level-1 and Level-2
subsets. These results confirm that the model trained with BalanceSFT
exhibits robust and consistent performance across diverse tool-calling
benchmarks.

### 4.4 Ablation Study

In the ablation study, all experiments are conducted under consistent
configurations to ensure fair and controlled comparisons. The basic SFT
method serves as the baseline to assess the contribution of each
proposed component. To further examine the generalization of our
proposed method framework, we conduct experiments on two base models:
Qwen2.5-Coder-Inst and Llama3.2-3B-Inst.

Effectiveness of the Designed Components. Our ablation analysis,
presented in Table
[5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
systematically investigates the effect of the two core
modules—Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB) loss and Hard Data
Re-sampling (HDR)—on both single-turn and multi-turn performance within
the BFCL benchmark.

For Qwen2.5-Coder-Inst, the SFT trained model achieves 81.73 and 38.25
in Single-Turn and Multi-Turn, respectively. Individual activation of
SSB yields improvements up to 82.20 (Single-Turn) and 41.62
(Multi-Turn). In contrast, applying SFT to HDR resampled data provides
larger gains, boosting Single-Turn by 2.12 and dramatically increasing
Multi-Turn by 4.87, suggesting that rare edge samples are critical.
Crucially, the combination of both SSB and HDR resulted in synergistic
gains, achieving the highest performance of 84.00 (Single-Turn) and
47.00 (Multi-Turn). These findings highlight the significant
contribution of both modules to improving model robustness and accuracy.

A similar pattern can be observed for Llama-3.2-3B-Inst, showing
consistent trends, which further validates the generality of our
approach. These results again validate that both SSB and HDR
individually enhance performance, especially in the Multi-Turn scenario.
Notably, their combination provides a complementary and superior method
for optimizing tool-use capabilities across different model
architectures, i.e., yielding more hard edge samples (through HDR) and
enabling the model to learn more effectively (through SSB).

### 4.5 Further Analysis

Comparison with Reinforcement Learning. To further validate the
effectiveness of the proposed BalanceSFT method, we compare it with
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [Guo et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib51) method on BFCL shown in
Table [4(a)](#S4.F4.sf1 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
the 7B and 3B models are trained upon Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Inst and
Llama-3.2-3B-Inst [Shao et al. (2024)](#bib.bib31). We use the
hyperparameter settings and reward design from the official GRPO
baseline described in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B RL Training Details ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness").
For Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Inst, the GRPO method achieves a higher score in
the Single-Turn task (84.60 vs. 84.00), but the BalanceSFT approach
outperforms it significantly in the Multi-Turn task (47.00 vs. 40.75).
This suggests that while GRPO maintains an edge in simpler, Single-Turn
interactions, the BalanceSFT method better enhances the model’s
capability to handle more complex, Multi-Turn dialogues. A similar trend
is observed with Llama-3.2-3B-Inst, where BalanceSFT outperforms GRPO in
both tasks, marginally in Single-Turn (78.99 vs. 77.78) and more notably
in Multi-Turn (36.12 vs. 34.00). The results indicate that the proposed
BalanceSFT approach provides a more balanced performance boost,
particularly excelling in the more challenging Multi-Turn setting
compared to the GRPO method, thereby validating its advantage in
enhancing model robustness across different interaction complexities.

Effectiveness of HDR Self-Evolving Loop. As shown in
Figure [4(c)](#S4.F4.sf3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
the model’s ability in Multi-Turn function call grows with the
Self-evolving Loop until convergence, providing strong evidence that the
proposed HDR can effectively and continuously sample complex edge
samples, driving the model performance toward a high-accuracy.

This improvement arises from the HDR Self-Evolving Loop, which forms a
self-reinforcing training cycle. HDR leverages model errors to create
harder edge samples that target its weak points, forming a focused
feedback loop for continual improvement. Through iterative refinement,
the model progressively enhances its accuracy, robustness across
complex, multi-step tasks.

Effectiveness of Alleviating Catastrophic Forgetting. To assess how
BalanceSFT impacts the coder model’s original coding capabilities, we
evaluate our model on widely recognized code generation benchmarks in
Figure [4(b)](#S4.F4.sf2 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
HumanEval and MBPP (including their plus variants) [Austin et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib46); [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib47); [Yu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib15). The results, presented in
Table [4(c)](#S4.F4.sf3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
demonstrate a crucial advantage of our method. Specifically,
BalanceSFT-7B maintains strong performance across all benchmarks, with
pass@1 scores only marginally lower (within 4%) compared to the base
Qwen2.5-Coder-Inst model. For instance, on HumanEval, BalanceSFT
achieves 0.841 compared to the base model’s 0.866, and on MBPP, it
reaches 0.794 versus 0.812. This minimal performance degradation stands
in stark contrast to models fine-tuned using standard SFT. The SFT
method shows dramatic drops in pass@1 scores on all the benchmarks,
notably falling from 0.866 to 0.470 on HumanEval and from 0.823 to 0.445
on HumanEval+.

These results indicate that BalanceSFT effectively mitigates
catastrophic forgetting, preserving the model’s original code
capabilities across benchmarks. This is because the SSB loss dynamically
rebalances the training signal, focusing updates on the concise, yet
crucial function call tokens. By concentrating learning on these key
tokens, the model avoids overfitting to lengthy reasoning and maintains
its original coding capabilities.

## 5 Conclusion

In this work, we identify two critical yet overlooked challenges in
standard SFT for function calling: the imbalance in training signals
between lengthy reasoning and concise function calls, and the scarcity
of hard training data. To address these issues, we propose BalanceSFT, a
novel framework that integrates a Self-adjusted Signal Balancing (SSB)
loss and a Hard Data Re-sampling (HDR) strategy. The SSB loss
dynamically recalibrates the learning focus between reasoning and
execution, while HDR iteratively enriches the training set with
high-quality complex examples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that
BalanceSFT enables a 7B model to achieve function calling performance
competitive with state-of-the-art giants like GPT-4o on BFCL and other
benchmarks. Our work provides a simple yet effective pathway toward more
robust and generalizable LLM-based tool use.

## Limitations

Despite its strong performance, BalanceSFT has two major limitations.
First, the effectiveness of the SSB loss depends on the initial quality
and structure of the CoT data, which may limit its applicability in
domains where high-quality reasoning annotations are scarce. Second,
while HDR improves data hardness, it relies on an ensemble of LLM judges
for quality control, which introduces computational cost and potential
bias from the judge models.

## Appendix A Dataset

Figure 5: API categories distribution of xlam-function-calling-60k and

different API categories.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: A Example for error in xlam dataset

### A.1 Data Analysis

Here, we split each turn of multi-turn conversations and count them
together with Single-Turn. By using Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct’s
tokenizer for token calculation, the average token length of function
call of the entire dataset (including rejections) is 31.07, the average
cot token length is 350.74. In the first data filtering, we obtain 85014
qualified simple data and 3178 difficult data for self-evolving,
dropping 1808 samples.

### A.2 Error in Dataset

As illustrated in
Figure [6](#A1.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix A Dataset ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
the xlam dataset contains an error in the formatting of function calls.
Specifically, an extra space appears between the opening bracket and the
function name ("\[ forecast_weather_api(…)"), which causes the Abstract
Syntax Tree (AST) parser to fail. This type of issue highlights the
importance of performing a base quality check on the dataset to ensure
correct syntax and reliable downstream processing. Ensuring proper
formatting is essential for both automated function call execution and
model evaluation.

## Appendix C More Results

### C.1 Full BFCL Single-Turn Results

We show the full single-turn results on the BFCL benchmark, where
BalanceSFT attains superior performance with scores of 88.29 and 79.70
on non-live and live sections. The results surpass most similar scale
models and achieve great enhancement on all the categories of live
section, which indicates that our model has achieved excellent
tool-calling capabilities under complex queries; the evaluation details
are shown in
Table [7](#A3.T7 "Table 7 ‣ C.1 Full BFCL Single-Turn Results ‣ Appendix C More Results ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness").

[TABLE]

Table 7: The evaluation details on BFCL benchmark (last updated August
26, 2025), with all metrics calculated using the official script.

### C.2 Results of Agentic Evaluation

In addition to single-turn and multi-turn function call capabilities,
BFCLv4 further evaluates the model’s agentic capability, specifically,
Web Search and Memory. We test our model on the corresponding test sets
in
Table [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ C.2 Results of Agentic Evaluation ‣ Appendix C More Results ‣ BalanceSFT: Improving LLM Function Calling with Balanced Training Signals and Data Hardness"),
even though our base model has almost no agentic capability and we do
not include any Web Search or Memory related data in the BalanceSFT
training, our model still shows improvement in these two evaluation
subsets, which indicates that our training and data selection are
beneficial to the model’s agentic ability.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | Web Search |  |  | Memory |  |  |  |
| Models | Overall | Base | No Snippet | Overall | KV | Vector | Recursive Sum |
| Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct | 4.50 | 4.00 | 5.00 | 2.37 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 7.10 |
| BalanceSFT-7B | 7.00 | 9.00 | 5.00 | 8.17 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 24.52 |

Table 8: Performance of model’s agentic ability.
````
